issues.legal_issue: The extraordinary criminal appellate jurisdiction permits interference when a judgment has caused grave injustice through material procedural unfairness or the misreading or unjustified disregard of important evidence.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a conviction affirmed by the High Court.
The High Court’s treatment of the defence witness and medical evidence contained errors that prejudiced the accused and contributed to a miscarriage of justice.
issues.conclusion: The case warranted interference under the extraordinary appellate jurisdiction because grave injustice had occurred.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court does not act as a general court of review or correct every error in a criminal case. It may intervene where the trial involved material illegality, procedural unfairness, or the judgment caused a miscarriage of justice by misreading or unjustifiably ignoring important evidence or relevant circumstances; the power is intended to be exercised where grave injustice is shown. No earlier case is cited for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_special_leave_appeal and (material_evidence_misread or important_evidence_ignored or procedural_unfairness) and grave_injustice

predicates.criminal_special_leave_appeal: The case is a criminal appeal seeking special leave to challenge a lower court judgment.
predicates.material_evidence_misread: The challenged judgment materially misreads important evidence.
predicates.important_evidence_ignored: The challenged judgment unjustifiably disregards important evidence or relevant circumstances.
predicates.procedural_unfairness: The proceedings involve material procedural illegality or unfairness to the accused.
predicates.grave_injustice: The errors or unfairness result in grave injustice.

issues.definition: When a criminal special leave appeal involves material evidentiary error or procedural unfairness resulting in grave injustice, the Supreme Court may intervene.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s testimony may be accepted in part even when the witness is disbelieved on another part of the account.
material_facts: The High Court rejected the prosecution witnesses’ account concerning the participation of two accused persons but accepted that they were present at the occurrence.
The appellant argued that rejection of their account about the other accused persons required rejection of their evidence against him as well.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected that argument, holding that disbelief of a witness on one matter does not require rejection of the witness’s testimony in its entirety; the evidence must be assessed carefully, part by part, in light of all relevant circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: A court must appraise the evidence in each case to determine which parts are worthy of acceptance. A witness’s exaggeration, imperfect memory, or unreliability on one matter does not establish a rule of law requiring rejection of all the witness’s evidence. The Court cited no provision or earlier case for this principle.

predicates.criminal_evidence_assessment: The court is assessing testimony in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.witness_disbelieved_on_one_part: The court finds a witness’s testimony unreliable concerning one part of the account.
predicates.other_testimony_requires_independent_ass: Other parts of the witness’s testimony must be evaluated on their own evidentiary merits and in the context of the case.

issues.definition: When a witness is disbelieved on one part of an account, the remaining testimony may still be accepted if independently assessed.

issues.legal_issue: A defence witness’s testimony cannot be summarily rejected merely because it conflicts with an earlier statement recorded during investigation when there is material supporting the witness’s account of police pressure.
material_facts: The injured witness was originally cited by the prosecution, whose investigating officer had obtained his statement during the investigation, but the prosecution later dropped him as having been won over.
The witness testified for the defence that police officers had beaten and pressured him and his father to support the prosecution.
The witness’s written complaint, his father’s application to a magistrate, and testimony from his uncle supported the allegations of police pressure.
The witness’s earlier investigative statement differed from his testimony in court.
issues.conclusion: In these circumstances, the earlier statement could not be treated as making the defence testimony necessarily false or as grounds to summarily discard it; the earlier statement deserved grave suspicion and the defence testimony had to be considered.
issues.legal_principle: The Court noted that a statement under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is normally recorded when the investigating agency considers a witness unwilling and wishes to pin the witness down. Where independent material supports allegations of police pressure, a conflicting earlier statement cannot by itself justify summarily rejecting the witness’s testimony in court. No earlier case is cited for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_trial_evidence and defence_witness_reports_police_pressure and pressure_supported_by_independent_material and earlier_investigative_statement_conflicts

predicates.criminal_trial_evidence: The court is assessing evidence in a criminal trial or appeal.
predicates.defence_witness_reports_police_pressure: A witness called for the defence testifies that police pressured or mistreated the witness to support the prosecution.
predicates.pressure_supported_by_independent_materi: Documents or other testimony support the allegation that police pressure occurred.
predicates.earlier_investigative_statement_conflict: The witness’s earlier statement recorded during investigation differs from the witness’s testimony in court.

issues.definition: When a defence witness describes police pressure and independent material supports that account, a conflicting earlier investigative statement alone does not justify summarily rejecting the court testimony.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court errs prejudicially by attributing a mistake to a medical expert on a material finding without a cogent evidentiary basis.
material_facts: The doctor who conducted the postmortem examination testified that the entry wounds on one deceased person showed tattooing and had earlier stated that the marks indicated a maximum firing distance of six feet.
The High Court considered that the doctor had mistaken another condition for tattooing, which affected its assessment of the firing distance.
The possibility that the doctor had made this mistake had not been put to him, and the record contained no cogent material establishing the proposed mistake.
issues.conclusion: The High Court grievously erred in imputing a mistake to the doctor without cogent material, and the error caused prejudice to the accused.
issues.legal_principle: A court may not displace material expert testimony by hypothesizing that the expert was mistaken without cogent evidentiary support. The Court relied on the evidence in the record and cited no provision or earlier case for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_review and expert_gave_material_opinion and appellate_court_hypothesized_expert_mistake and no_cogent_basis_for_mistake

predicates.criminal_appeal_review: The court is reviewing evidence in a criminal appeal.
predicates.expert_gave_material_opinion: An expert gave an opinion material to a disputed issue.
predicates.appellate_court_hypothesized_expert_mist: The appellate court attributed the expert’s opinion to a mistake.
predicates.no_cogent_basis_for_mistake: The record contains no cogent evidence supporting the proposed mistake.

issues.definition: When an appellate court rejects a material expert opinion by hypothesizing a mistake without cogent support, that rejection is prejudicial error.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction cannot stand when the prosecution has not proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt and the evidence raises reasonable doubt about whether the accused was the aggressor.
material_facts: The High Court treated one witness as a false witness who had not seen the occurrence, leaving no accepted eyewitness account of the first shot at the first deceased.

The injured witness testified for the defence that the accused fired after being challenged and attacked, and evidence from the witness and his family supported allegations that police had pressured them to support the prosecution.
The doctor’s evidence about tattooing on the wounds was not properly displaced by the High Court’s unsupported hypothesis of mistake.

The Court found an important lacuna in the prosecution case and concluded that the defence evidence, considered with the accused’s statement, appeared to negate the prosecution claim that the accused was the aggressor.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution had not proved the murder beyond reasonable doubt. The accused was acquitted, and the conviction under the Arms Act was also set aside on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Where the evidence leaves an important lacuna and the defence evidence raises reasonable doubt about the prosecution account, the accused is entitled to the benefit of that doubt. The Court applied Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, Section 27 of the Indian Arms Act, and Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in considering the charges and the accused’s account; it cited no earlier case for the benefit-of-doubt ruling.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The case is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.prosecution_case_has_material_lacuna: The prosecution evidence leaves an important gap in proving the accused’s guilt.
predicates.defence_evidence_raises_reasonable_doubt: The defence evidence, considered with the other evidence, raises reasonable doubt about whether the accused was the aggressor.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a criminal conviction, an important gap in the prosecution case together with defence evidence raising reasonable doubt entitles the accused to acquittal.
